message.content:
Lions (Panthera leo) and zebras (Equus quagga) belong to very different mammalian lineages—Felidae (Carnivora) and Equidae (Perissodactyla).  
Their most recent common ancestor is therefore not a specific “species” you can name, but rather a **placental mammal that lived roughly 90–100 million years ago**.  

That ancestor would have been a small, insect‑eating mammal that lived in the late Cretaceous/early Paleogene and gave rise to the entire Laurasiatherian clade, which later split into the lineages that became carnivores (including lions) and odd‑toed ungulates (including zebras).
message.reasoning:
The user asks: "What is the common ancestor of lion and zebra?" They want a biological answer. The common ancestor of lion (Panthera leo) and zebra (Equus quagga) would be a common ancestor in the mammalian lineage. Both are mammals, but lions are felids (family Felidae), zebras are equids (family Equidae). They diverged from a common ancestor in the order Carnivora vs Perissodactyla? Actually lions are in order Carnivora, suborder Feliformia. Zebras are in order Perissodactyla (odd-toed ungulates). So their common ancestor would be a more distant mammalian ancestor, perhaps a placental mammal ancestor. The last common ancestor of all placental mammals is the eutherian ancestor. But maybe they want the last common ancestor of the two species: that would be the last common ancestor of the families Felidae and Equidae, which is the last common ancestor of the order Carnivora and Perissodactyla. That would be the last common ancestor of the clade that includes both orders, which is the clade of Laurasiatheria? Actually Carnivora and Perissodactyla are both part of the clade Laurasiatheria. So the last common ancestor of lions and zebras would be the last common ancestor of Laurasiatheria, which is a placental mammal that lived about 90-100 million years ago. So the answer: the last common ancestor of the two species is a mammal that lived around 90-100 million years ago, likely a small, insectivorous mammal. But maybe they want the common ancestor of the two species: the last common ancestor of the families Felidae and Equidae is the last common ancestor of the order Carnivora and Perissodactyla, which is the last common ancestor of Laurasiatheria. So answer: a small, insectivorous mammal from the late Cretaceous/Eocene. Or we can say: the last common ancestor of lions and zebras is the last common ancestor of all placental mammals, which is the ancestor of Laurasiatheria. But the question: "What is the common ancestor of lion and zebra?" Might be answered: "They share a common ancestor that lived about 90 million years ago, the last common ancestor of the Laurasiatheria clade." Or "the last common ancestor of the two species is a small, insectivorous mammal that lived in the late Cretaceous." So answer accordingly.
